title: Reliable Entropy Estimation From Observed Statistics For Device-Independent Quantum Cryptography
authors: Gereon Koßmann And René Schwonnek
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2238 (2026).

We introduce a numerical framework for reliably estimating conditional von Neumann entropies, a central quantity in device-independent quantum cryptography and randomness generation. Our method is based on semidefinite relaxations derived from the Navascués--Pironio--Acín hierarchy and provides entropy bounds directly from observed statistics, assuming only the validity of quantum mechanics. The approach builds on a recent integral representation of entropy and substantially improves efficiency: it requires about half as many support variables as existing methods, while allowing these variables to be chosen projectively, leading to a significant reduction in runtime. These advances enable the practical certification of randomness and security even in noisy conditions, while integrating seamlessly with modern entropy accumulation theorems. Consequently, our framework becomes a versatile tool for quantum cryptographic protocols, broadening the possibilities for secure communication in untrusted environments.

.
tldr: The paper introduces an efficient numerical framework for estimating conditional von Neumann entropies directly from observed statistics in device-independent quantum cryptography.
motivation: Device-independent cryptography and randomness generation require reliable lower bounds on conditional von Neumann entropy under untrusted devices, using only observed statistics and quantum mechanics.
method: The authors develop semidefinite relaxations based on the Navascués–Pironio–Acín hierarchy, combined with an integral representation of entropy, and use projectively chosen support variables to reduce computational cost.
result: The method requires about half as many support variables as existing approaches and significantly reduces runtime, enabling practical randomness and security certification even in noisy conditions.
conclusion: This framework provides a versatile and efficient tool for device-independent quantum cryptographic protocols and integrates with modern entropy accumulation theorems.

title: The Three Kinds Of Three-qubit Entanglement
authors: Szilárd Szalay
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2242 (2026).

We construct an important missing piece in the entanglement theory of pure three-qubit states, which is a polynomial measure of W-entanglement. This works in parallel to the three-tangle, which is a polynomial measure of GHZ-entanglement, and to the bipartite concurrence, which is a polynomial measure of bipartite entanglement. We also show that these entanglement measures are ordered, the bipartite measure is larger than the W measure, which is larger than the GHZ measure. It is meaningful then to consider these three types of three-qubit entanglement, which are also ordered, bipartite is weaker than W, which is weaker than GHZ, in parallel to the order of the three kinds of equivalence classes of entangled three-qubit states.

.
tldr: The paper constructs a polynomial measure of W-entanglement for pure three-qubit states and shows an ordering among bipartite, W, and GHZ entanglement measures.
motivation: Three-qubit entanglement theory lacked a polynomial measure for W-type entanglement analogous to the three-tangle for GHZ entanglement and concurrence for bipartite entanglement.
method: The author defines a polynomial entanglement measure for W-class pure three-qubit states and compares it with the three-tangle and bipartite concurrence, establishing ordering relations among the measures and corresponding entanglement types.
result: The new W-entanglement measure completes the trio of polynomial measures, and the measures are ordered as bipartite concurrence ≥ W measure ≥ three-tangle, matching the ordering of bipartite, W, and GHZ entanglement classes.
conclusion: The work fills an important gap in pure three-qubit entanglement theory by providing a unified polynomial characterization of the three entanglement kinds and clarifying their hierarchy.

title: Requirements For Teleportation In An Intercity Quantum Network
authors: Soubhadra Maiti, Guus Avis, Sounak Kar And Stephanie Wehner
abstract: We investigate the hardware requirements for quantum teleportation in an intercity-scale network topology consisting of two metropolitan-scale networks connected via a long-distance backbone link. Specifically, we identify the minimal improvements required beyond the state-of-the-art to achieve an end-to-end expected teleportation fidelity of , which represents the classical limit. To this end, we formulate the hardware requirements computation as optimisation problems, where the hardware parameters representing the underlying device capabilities serve as decision variables. Assuming a simplified noise model, we derive closed-form analytical expressions for the teleportation fidelity and rate when the network is realised using heterogeneous quantum hardware, including a quantum repeater chain with a memory cut-off. Our derivations are based on events defined by the order statistics of link generation durations in both the metropolitan networks and the backbone, and the resulting expressions are verified against NetSquid simulations. The analytical expressions facilitate efficient exploration of the optimisation parameter space without resorting to computationally intensive simulations. We then apply this framework to a representative realisation in which the metropolitan nodes are based on trapped-ion processors and the backbone is composed of ensemble-based quantum memories. Our results suggest that teleportation across metropolitan distances already reaches the classical limit with state-of-the-art hardware when the data qubit is prepared after end-to-end entanglement has been established, whereas extending teleportation to intercity scales requires additional, though plausibly achievable, improvements in hardware performance.
tldr: This paper derives analytical expressions and optimization methods for teleportation fidelity and rate in an intercity quantum network using heterogeneous repeater hardware.
motivation: Intercity-scale quantum teleportation requires understanding the hardware improvements needed beyond current state-of-the-art, especially when combining metropolitan networks with a long-distance backbone.
method: The authors model hardware requirements as optimization problems with device parameters as decision variables, derive closed-form expressions for teleportation fidelity and rate using order statistics of link generation durations, and verify results with NetSquid simulations.
result: For a representative network with trapped-ion metropolitan nodes and ensemble-based quantum memories in the backbone, teleportation over metropolitan distances can reach the classical limit with state-of-the-art hardware when data qubits are prepared after entanglement distribution, while intercity scales require additional but plausible hardware improvements.
conclusion: The framework enables efficient exploration of hardware parameter space for intercity quantum networks and identifies necessary improvements for end-to-end teleportation at larger scales.

title: Macroscopic Quantum Coherence And Entanglement In Mechanical Systems
authors: Benjamin Yadin And Matteo Fadel
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2257 (2026).

The notion of a macroscopic quantum state must be pinned down in order to assess how well experiments probe the large-scale limits of quantum mechanics. However, the issue of quantifying so-called quantum macroscopicity is fraught with multiple approaches having varying interpretations and levels of computability and measurability. Here, we introduce two measures that capture independent macroscopic properties: i) extensive size, measuring the degree of coherence in position or momentum observables relative to atomic-scale units, and ii) entangled size, quantifying the number of entangled subsystems. These measures unify many desirable features of past proposals while having rigorously justified interpretations from quantum information theory in terms of coherence and multipartite entanglement. We demonstrate how to estimate them and obtain lower-bounds using experimental data from micro-mechanical oscillators and diffracting molecules. Notably, we find evidence for genuine multipartite entanglement of [MATH] to [MATH] atoms in recent mechanical superposition states.

.
tldr: The paper introduces two quantum-information-based measures of macroscopicity—extensive size and entangled size—and applies them to mechanical superposition experiments.
motivation: There is no consensus on how to quantify macroscopic quantum states, and existing macroscopicity measures vary in interpretation, computability, and measurability.
method: The authors define measures based on coherence in position/momentum relative to atomic scales and on the number of entangled subsystems, with rigorous interpretations in terms of coherence and multipartite entanglement, and derive lower bounds estimable from experimental data.
result: They estimate the measures using data from micro-mechanical oscillators and diffracting molecules, finding evidence for genuine multipartite entanglement involving roughly 10^? to 10^? atoms in recent mechanical superposition states.
conclusion: The proposed measures unify desirable features of prior macroscopicity proposals while providing operationally meaningful, experimentally accessible characterizations of macroscopic quantum coherence and entanglement.

title: Certified Bounds On Optimization Problems In Quantum Theory
authors: Younes Naceur, Jie Wang, Victor Magron, And Antonio Acín
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2254 (2026).

Semidefinite relaxations of polynomial optimization have become a central tool for addressing the non-convex optimization problems over non-commutative operators that are ubiquitous in quantum information theory and, more in general, quantum physics. Yet, as these global relaxation methods are solved numerically, the bounds issued by the semidefinite solver can – and often do – exceed the global optimum, undermining their certifiability. To counter this issue, we introduce a framework for extracting rigorous certified bounds on non-commutative optimization problems from inexact numerical data, and apply it to several paradigmatic problems in quantum information theory. An extension to sparsity and symmetry-adapted semidefinite relaxations is also provided and compared to the general dense scheme. Our results establish rational post-processing as a practical route to reliable certification, pushing semidefinite optimization toward a certifiable standard for quantum information science.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a framework for extracting rigorous certified bounds from numerical semidefinite relaxations of non-commutative polynomial optimization problems in quantum information theory.
motivation: Semidefinite relaxations are widely used to bound non-convex optimization problems over quantum operators, but numerical solver inaccuracies can produce non-certifiable bounds that exceed the true optimum.
method: The authors develop rational post-processing techniques to convert inexact numerical semidefinite programming data into rigorous certified bounds, and extend the approach to sparsity- and symmetry-adapted relaxation schemes.
result: The framework is applied to several paradigmatic quantum information problems, yielding certified bounds and demonstrating that rational post-processing is a practical route to reliable certification.
conclusion: The work pushes semidefinite optimization toward a certifiable standard for quantum information science, making numerical bounds trustworthy for rigorous quantum-theoretic analyses.

title: Work Statistics Of Sudden Quantum Quenches: A Random Matrix Theory Perspective On Gaussianity And Its Deviations
authors: Miguel Tierz
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2241 (2026).

We show that, for sudden quenches, the work distribution reduces to the statistics of the traces of powers of Haar unitaries, which are random unitary matrices drawn uniformly from the unitary group. For translation-invariant quadratic fermionic chains with interactions extending to [MATH] neighbors and periodic boundary conditions, the Loschmidt amplitude admits a unitary matrix model / Toeplitz representation, which yields a work variable of the form [MATH] (and in models with pairing terms -superconducting pairing- additional [MATH] terms appear). By invoking multivariate central limit theorems for vectors of traces of unitaries, we obtain a Gaussian distribution for [MATH] with variance [MATH] and asymptotic independence across different powers. We also characterise the conditions under which non-Gaussian tails arise, for example from many interaction terms or their slow decay, as well as the appearance of Fisher-Hartwig singularities. We illustrate these mechanisms in the XY chain. Various numerical diagnostics support the analytical results.

.
tldr: The paper analyzes work statistics for sudden quantum quenches using random matrix theory, showing Gaussian work distributions for translation-invariant quadratic fermionic chains and characterizing non-Gaussian deviations.
motivation: Work statistics in non-equilibrium quantum quenches are central to quantum thermodynamics, but a general random-matrix understanding of when Gaussianity emerges or fails is lacking.
method: The authors map sudden-quench work distributions to traces of powers of Haar-random unitaries, represent the Loschmidt amplitude via unitary matrix models and Toeplitz determinants, and apply multivariate central limit theorems to obtain Gaussian statistics.
result: They derive Gaussian work distributions with explicit variance and asymptotic independence across powers, and identify conditions for non-Gaussian tails such as many interaction terms, slow decay, and Fisher-Hartwig singularities, illustrated in the XY chain with numerical diagnostics.
conclusion: The work provides a random-matrix framework for sudden-quench work statistics, clarifying Gaussian and non-Gaussian regimes and linking them to universality classes and singularity structure.

title: Quantum Authenticated Key Expansion With Key Recycling
authors: Wen Yu Kon, Jefferson Chu, Kevin Han Yong Loh, Obada Alia, Omar Amer, Marco Pistoia, Kaushik Chakraborty, And Charles Lim
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2255 (2026).

Data privacy and authentication are two main security requirements for remote access and cloud services. While QKD has been explored to address data privacy concerns, oftentimes its use is separate from the client authentication protocol despite implicitly providing authentication. Here, we present a quantum authentication key expansion (QAKE) protocol that (1) integrates both authentication and key expansion within a single protocol, and (2) provides key recycling property – allowing all authentication keys to be reused. We analyse the security of the protocol in a QAKE framework adapted from a classical authentication key exchange (AKE) framework, providing separate security conditions for authentication and data privacy. We experimentally implemented the protocol with appropriate post-selection. Additional results on the security of pseudorandom basis generation in QAKE and decoy state BB84 are provided.

.
tldr: The authors introduce a quantum authenticated key expansion (QAKE) protocol that unifies client authentication with key expansion and provably permits recycling of all authentication keys.
motivation: Data privacy and authentication are both essential for remote access and cloud services, yet QKD-based privacy solutions are typically decoupled from client authentication protocols even though they implicitly provide authentication; integrating the two while avoiding authentication-key exhaustion is the goal.
method: They define a QAKE framework adapted from classical authenticated key exchange (AKE) frameworks, giving separate security conditions for authentication and data privacy, and experimentally implement the protocol with appropriate post-selection; they further analyze the security of pseudorandom basis generation in QAKE and in decoy-state BB84.
result: The protocol achieves joint authentication and key expansion with full key recycling, and the accompanying analyses establish security conditions for authentication and privacy as well as bounds on pseudorandom basis generation in both QAKE and decoy-state BB84.
conclusion: QAKE shows that authentication and key expansion can be combined in a single protocol without consuming authentication keys, backed by a modular security framework and experimental validation, making it attractive for practical secure remote access.

title: A General Framework For Gradient-Based Optimization Of Superconducting Quantum Circuits Using Qubit Discovery As A Case Study
authors: Taha Rajabzadeh, Alex Boulton-Mckeehan, Sam Bonkowsky, David I. Schuster, And Amir H. Safavi-Naeini
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2249 (2026).

Engineering the Hamiltonian of a quantum system is fundamental to the design of quantum systems. Automating Hamiltonian design through gradient-based optimization can dramatically accelerate this process. However, computing the gradients of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a Hamiltonian–a large, sparse matrix–relative to system properties poses a significant challenge, especially for arbitrary systems. Superconducting quantum circuits offer substantial flexibility in Hamiltonian design, making them an ideal platform for this task. In this work, we present a comprehensive framework for the gradient-based optimization of superconducting quantum circuits, leveraging the SQcircuit software package. By addressing the challenge of calculating the gradient of the eigensystem for large, sparse Hamiltonians and integrating automatic differentiation within SQcircuit, our framework enables efficient and precise computation of gradients for various circuit properties or custom-defined metrics, streamlining the optimization process. We apply this framework to the qubit discovery problem, demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying qubit designs with superior performance metrics. The optimized circuits show improvements in a heuristic measure of gate count, upper bounds on gate speed, decoherence time, and resilience to noise and fabrication errors compared to existing qubits. While this methodology is showcased through qubit optimization and discovery, it is versatile and can be extended to tackle other optimization challenges in superconducting quantum hardware design.

.
tldr: The paper presents a gradient-based optimization framework for superconducting quantum circuit Hamiltonians and applies it to automated qubit discovery.
motivation: Engineering Hamiltonians is central to quantum hardware design, but computing gradients of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of large sparse Hamiltonians is challenging, limiting automated optimization of superconducting circuits.
method: The authors develop a framework for differentiating eigensystems of large sparse Hamiltonians and integrate automatic differentiation into the SQcircuit software package to optimize circuit properties or custom metrics.
result: Applied to qubit discovery, the framework identifies circuit designs with improved heuristic gate count, gate-speed upper bounds, decoherence time, and resilience to noise and fabrication errors compared with existing qubits.
conclusion: The methodology provides a versatile tool for superconducting quantum hardware design and can be extended beyond qubit discovery to other circuit optimization problems.

title: Asymptotically Good Bosonic Fock State Codes
authors: Dor Elimelech, Arda Aydin, And Alexander Barg
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2240 (2026).

We study the error-correction properties of multi-mode Fock-state codes under amplitude-damping (AD) noise, focusing on the asymptotic regime in which the total excitation of the code states grows without limit and the number of photon losses induced by the noise scales linearly with it. In this setting, existing code families, which correct only sublinearly many photon losses, do not protect against amplitude-damping (AD) noise with a constant loss parameter. As our main result, we address this gap by constructing asymptotically good Fock-state codes relying on random classical codes in the discrete simplex. Unlike many standard constructions of random quantum codes, our construction introduces randomness through the underlying classical indexing structure. Randomization also enables another desirable feature: bounded per-mode occupancy, which limits the number of photons in any individual mode and thereby increases the coherence lifetime of the code states. Finally, via a relation between Fock-state codes and permutation-invariant codes, our results also yield asymptotically good families of qudit permutation-invariant codes as well as codes in monolithic nuclear state spaces.

.
tldr: The paper constructs asymptotically good multi-mode Fock-state codes that protect against amplitude-damping noise with a constant loss parameter, using random classical codes in the discrete simplex.
motivation: Existing Fock-state code families only correct sublinearly many photon losses and fail against amplitude-damping noise with a constant loss parameter in the asymptotic regime.
method: The authors introduce randomness through an underlying classical indexing structure based on random classical codes in the discrete simplex, and relate Fock-state codes to permutation-invariant codes.
result: The construction yields asymptotically good Fock-state codes with bounded per-mode occupancy, and also produces asymptotically good qudit permutation-invariant codes and codes in monolithic nuclear state spaces.
conclusion: The work closes a gap in bosonic error correction by providing asymptotically good Fock-state codes for constant-rate amplitude-damping noise and broadens the scope of permutation-invariant quantum codes.

title: Strict Hierarchy Between $n$-wise Measurement Simulability, Compatibility Structures, And Multi-copy Compatibility
authors: Lucas Tendick, Costantino Budroni, And Marco Túlio Quintino
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2231 (2026).

The incompatibility of quantum measurements, i.e. the fact that certain observable quantities cannot be measured jointly is widely regarded as a distinctive quantum feature with important implications for the foundations and the applications of quantum information theory. While the standard incompatibility of multiple measurements has been the focus of attention since the inception of quantum theory, its generalizations, such as measurement simulability, [MATH]-wise incompatibility, and mulit-copy incompatibility have only been proposed recently. Here, we point out that all these generalizations are differing notions of the question of how many measurements are genuinely contained in a measurement device. We then show, that all notions do differ not only in their operational meaning but also mathematically in the set of measurement assemblages they describe. We then fully resolve the relations between these different generalizations, by showing a strict hierarchy between these notions. Hence, we provide a general framework for generalized measurement incompatibility. Finally, we consider the implications our results have for recent works using these different notions.

.
tldr: The paper establishes a strict hierarchy among generalized notions of measurement incompatibility, including n-wise measurement simulability, compatibility structures, and multi-copy compatibility.
motivation: Measurement incompatibility is a distinctive quantum feature central to foundations and applications, but recent generalizations have lacked a unified comparison.
method: The authors interpret these generalizations as different answers to how many measurements are genuinely contained in a measurement device and compare the corresponding sets of measurement assemblages.
result: They prove that the notions differ both operationally and mathematically, yielding a strict hierarchy and a general framework for generalized measurement incompatibility.
conclusion: The results clarify the relations between these concepts and their implications for recent works using different notions of measurement incompatibility.

title: Noncontextuality Inequalities For Prepare-transform-measure Scenarios
authors: David Schmid, Roberto D. Baldijão, John H. Selby, Ana Belén Sainz, And Robert W. Spekkens
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2250 (2026).

We provide the first systematic technique for deriving witnesses of contextuality in prepare-transform-measure scenarios. More specifically, we show how linear quantifier elimination can be used to compute a polytope of correlations consistent with generalized noncontextuality in such scenarios. This polytope is specified as a set of noncontextuality inequalities that are necessary and sufficient conditions for observed data in the scenario to admit of a classical explanation relative to any linear operational identities, if one ignores some constraints from diagram preservation. While including these latter constraints generally leads to tighter inequalities, it seems that nonlinear quantifier elimination would be required to systematically include them. We also provide a linear program which can certify the nonclassicality of a set of numerical data arising in a prepare-transform-measure experiment. We apply our results to get a robust noncontextuality inequality for transformations that can be violated within the stabilizer subtheory. Finally, we give a simple algorithm for computing all the linear operational identities holding among a given set of states, of transformations, or of measurements.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a systematic linear quantifier elimination method to derive noncontextuality inequalities for prepare-transform-measure scenarios and applies it to obtain robust contextuality witnesses, including one violated in the stabilizer subtheory.
motivation: Witnessing contextuality in prepare-transform-measure scenarios lacks a general systematic technique, limiting both foundational tests and applications to quantum computation subtheories such as the stabilizer formalism.
method: The authors use linear quantifier elimination to compute the polytope of correlations consistent with generalized noncontextuality under linear operational identities, provide a linear program for certifying nonclassicality, and give an algorithm for enumerating linear operational identities.
result: They derive noncontextuality inequalities that are necessary and sufficient for classical explainability under linear operational identities (up to diagram-preservation constraints) and obtain a robust inequality for transformations violated within the stabilizer subtheory.
conclusion: The work provides a practical framework for deriving and testing noncontextuality inequalities in prepare-transform-measure experiments, with potential applications to contextuality in quantum computation and foundational tests.

title: Noise-induced Thermalization In Quantum Systems
authors: Sameer Dambal, Yu Zhang, Eric R Bittner And Pavan Hosur
abstract: In the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum era, noise is widely regarded as the primary obstacle to achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation. However, certain stages of the quantum computing pipeline can, in fact, benefit from this noise. In this work, we exploit the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis to show that an number of noise occurrences can accelerate a fundamental task in quantum computing—the preparation of Gibbs states. We demonstrate this behavior using classical simulations with Haar-random and phase-flip noise, respectively, on a spin-1/2 chain with a local Hamiltonian. Our non-integrable model sees faster thermalization in the presence of noise, while our integrable model reaches a state that lies between a generalized Gibbs state and a Gibbs state due to noise. Since certifying a local Gibbs state is relatively easy on a quantum computer, our approach provides a new practical solution to a key problem in quantum computing. More broadly, these results establish a new paradigm in which noise can be harnessed on quantum computers, enabling practical advantages before the years of fault-tolerance.
tldr: The paper uses the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis to show that noise can accelerate Gibbs state preparation in quantum systems.
motivation: In the noisy intermediate-scale quantum era, noise is typically seen as an obstacle, but certain computational tasks may actually benefit from it.
method: Classical simulations of Haar-random and phase-flip noise on a spin-1/2 chain with a local Hamiltonian are used to compare non-integrable and integrable models.
result: The non-integrable model thermalizes faster in the presence of noise, while the integrable model reaches a state between a generalized Gibbs state and a Gibbs state.
conclusion: Noise can be harnessed as a resource for practical quantum computing advantages before fault tolerance is achieved.

title: Approach To Optimal Quantum Transport Via States Over Time
authors: Matt Hoogsteder-Riera, John Calsamiglia, And Andreas Winter
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2236 (2026).

We approach the problem of constructing a quantum analogue of the immensely fruitful classical transport cost theory of Monge from a new angle. Going back to the original motivations, by which the transport is a bilinear function of a mass distribution (without loss of generality a probability density) and a transport plan (a stochastic kernel), we explore the quantum version where the mass distribution is generalised to a density matrix, and the transport plan to a completely positive and trace preserving map. These two data are naturally integrated into their Jordan product, which is called state over time (“stote''), and the transport cost is postulated to be a linear function of it. We explore the properties of this transport cost, as well as the optimal transport cost between two given states (simply the minimum cost over all suitable transport plans). After that, we analyse in considerable detail the case of unitary invariant cost, for which we can calculate many costs analytically. These findings suggest that our quantum transport cost is qualitatively different from Monge's classical transport.

.
tldr: The paper develops a quantum analogue of Monge transport theory using density matrices as mass distributions, CPTP maps as transport plans, and the Jordan product 'state over time' to define a linear transport cost.
motivation: Classical optimal transport has been highly fruitful, motivating a principled quantum version that preserves the bilinear structure of mass distribution and transport plan.
method: The authors generalize mass distributions to density matrices and transport plans to completely positive trace-preserving maps, integrate them via the Jordan product into a 'state over time', and define transport cost as a linear functional of this object.
result: They characterize properties of the quantum transport cost and the optimal transport cost between states, and analytically compute many costs in the unitary-invariant case.
conclusion: The framework suggests that quantum transport cost is qualitatively different from classical Monge transport, opening a new direction in quantum information theory.

title: Towards Quantum Computing Feynman Diagrams In Hybrid Qubit-oscillator Devices
authors: S. Varona, S. Saner, O. Bäzävan, G. Araneda, G. Aarts, And A. Bermudez
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2252 (2026).

We show that recent experiments in hybrid qubit-oscillator devices that measure the phase-space characteristic function of the oscillator via the qubit can be seen through the lens of functional calculus and path integrals, drawing a clear analogy with the generating functional of a quantum field theory. This connection suggests an expansion of the characteristic function in terms of Feynman diagrams, exposing the role of the real-time bosonic propagator, and identifying the external source functions with certain time-dependent couplings that can be controlled experimentally. By applying maximum-likelihood techniques, we show that the “measurement'' of these Feynman diagrams can be reformulated as a problem of multi-parameter point estimation that takes as input a set of Ramsey-type measurements of the qubit. By numerical simulations that consider leading imperfections in trapped-ion devices, we identify the optimal regimes in which Feynman diagrams could be reconstructed from measured data with low systematic and stochastic errors. We discuss how these ideas can be generalized to finite temperatures via the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, contributing to a bottom-up approach to probe quantum simulators of lattice field theories by systematically increasing the qubit-oscillator number.

.
tldr: The authors reinterpret phase-space characteristic-function measurements in hybrid qubit-oscillator devices as a Feynman-diagram expansion of a generating functional, and show how to reconstruct these diagrams from Ramsey-type qubit measurements.
motivation: Recent experiments couple qubits to oscillators to probe bosonic phase-space distributions, but a systematic field-theoretic framework connecting these measurements to propagators and source terms is lacking.
method: They map the measured characteristic function onto the generating functional of a quantum field theory, expand it in Feynman diagrams with real-time bosonic propagators and experimentally controllable source couplings, and cast diagram estimation as multi-parameter point estimation using maximum-likelihood on simulated Ramsey measurements with trapped-ion imperfections.
result: Numerical simulations identify regimes where leading Feynman diagrams can be reconstructed with low systematic and stochastic errors, and the approach is extended to finite temperature via the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism.
conclusion: The work offers a bottom-up route to characterize and probe quantum simulators of lattice field theories through scaling qubit-oscillator hybrid devices.

title: Composable Logical Gate Error In Approximate Quantum Error Correction: Reexamining Gate Implementations In Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Codes
authors: Lukas Brenner, Beatriz Dias, And Robert Koenig
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2230 (2026).

Quantifying the accuracy of logical gates is paramount in approximate error correction, where perfect implementations are often unachievable with the available set of physical operations. To this end, we introduce a single scalar quantity we call the (composable) logical gate error. It captures both the deviation of the logical action from the desired target gate as well as leakage out of the code space. It is subadditive under successive application of gates, providing a simple means for analyzing circuits. We show how to bound the composable logical gate error in terms of matrix elements of physical unitaries between (approximate) logical computational basis states. In the continuous-variable context, this sidesteps the need for computing energy-bounded norms. As an example, we study the composable logical gate error for linear optics implementations of Paulis and Cliffords in approximate Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes. We find that the logical gate error for implementations of Paulis depends linearly on the squeezing parameter. This implies that their accuracy improves monotonically with the amount of squeezing. For some Cliffords, however, linear optics implementations which are exact for ideal GKP codes fail in the approximate case: they have a constant logical gate error even in the limit of infinite squeezing. This is consistent with previous results about the limitations of certain gate implementations for approximate GKP codes. It shows that findings applicable to ideal GKP codes do not always translate to the realm of physically realizable approximate GKP codes.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a composable logical gate error metric for approximate quantum error correction and analyzes linear-optics gate implementations in approximate GKP codes.
motivation: Logical gate accuracy is difficult to quantify in approximate error correction, where physical operations cannot realize ideal logical gates and leakage out of the code space must be accounted for.
method: The authors define a single scalar composable logical gate error that includes target-gate deviation and code-space leakage, prove subadditivity under gate composition, and bound it using matrix elements of physical unitaries between approximate logical basis states.
result: For linear-optics implementations of Paulis and Cliffords in approximate GKP codes, Pauli gate error scales linearly with the squeezing parameter, while some Clifford implementations that are exact for ideal GKP codes have constant error even at infinite squeezing.
conclusion: The composable logical gate error provides a practical circuit-level accuracy measure for approximate QEC, and shows that ideal-GKP gate implementations do not always remain accurate in physically realizable approximate GKP codes.

title: Finite Quantum Pumps For Phase-locked Parametric Amplification: Requirements For Quantum-battery Work Sources
authors: Borhan Ahmadi
abstract: Quantum batteries have been proposed as locally precharged work sources for superconducting quantum technologies, suggesting a route to reduce continuously supplied microwave drives. Here we ask what a finite bosonic pump must provide to replace the pump tone of a nondegenerate parametric amplifier during a readout window. Quantizing the pump exposes a resource distinction hidden in the classical description: stored energy and the ordinary marginal signal response can survive pump phase twirling, whereas a reproducible phase-locked signal-idler field requires pump coherences in the number sectors coupled by the mixing process. In a closed trilinear model, a coherent pump and its number-matched phase-twirled counterpart generate the same number-like marginal observables, but only the coherent pump produces anomalous two-mode coherence and an EPR-squeezed interference dip. Including leakage, we collect the emitted fields into cascaded temporal modes. At matched collector bandwidth, the coherent pump gives the interference certifier , whereas the phase-randomized control gives . A weak seeded-signal analysis shows more sharply that an exact pump phase twirl leaves the collected signal marginal invariant by phase covariance while eliminating the anomalous signal-idler coherence. A finite-cutoff scan also indicates that weak amplitude squeezing can modestly deepen the phase-sensitive dip by reducing pump-number fluctuations while preserving most of the coherent displacement. Thus, for the three-wave-mixing pump families studied here, adjacent-number pump coherence is the resource that establishes a phase-locked joint amplifier field, rather than a prerequisite for energy transfer or ordinary marginal signal response.
tldr: The paper analyzes finite quantized bosonic pumps for phase-locked parametric amplification, identifying pump number-sector coherence as the key resource for generating a reproducible signal-idler field.
motivation: Quantum batteries are proposed as local work sources for superconducting technologies, but it is unclear what a finite pump must supply to replace a continuous pump tone in parametric-amplifier readout.
method: The author studies a closed trilinear model with a quantized pump, comparing coherent pumps with phase-twirled controls, and extends the analysis to leakage by collecting emitted fields into cascaded temporal modes.
result: A coherent pump and its number-matched phase-twirled counterpart agree in number-like marginal observables, but only the coherent pump produces anomalous two-mode coherence and an EPR-squeezed interference dip; weak amplitude squeezing can modestly deepen the dip.
conclusion: For the studied three-wave-mixing pump families, adjacent-number pump coherence is the resource enabling a phase-locked joint amplifier field, rather than a prerequisite for energy transfer or ordinary marginal signal response.

title: Transcendental Momentum Quantization In Rashba Nanowires And Zero Energy States In Their Normal And Superconducting Phase
authors: Nico Leumer, Harald Schmid, Milena Grifoni And Magdalena Marganska
abstract: We study finite system properties of the canonical low energy model for a semiconducting nanowire with Rashba spin–orbit coupling (SOC). The case of an isolated wire as well as of one proximitized by an s-wave superconductor are considered. Already for the normal wire, the presence of SOC leads to eigenstates of the finite system composed of more than two momentum eigenstates. The exact quantization condition for the wavevectors is not that of a quantum box, but given instead by a transcendental equation linking the involved wavevectors. For the wire with superconducting pairing, the presence of electron and hole channels complicates the composition of the eigenstates. In this case we derive an approximate quantization condition close to the phase boundary, and an approximate condition for the appearance of exact zero energy states. It can be satisfied both in the topological and in the trivial phase. Both the trivial and topological zero energy states contribute to the linear transport through Andreev reflection and direct transmission processes, with their relative importance depending on the degree of the states’ localization at the boundary. A negative spin-flip interference contribution causes trivial zero-energy states to exhibit a zero-bias conductance plateau, whereas Majorana zero modes (MZM) display a peak. This distinct lineshape may serve as an experimental signature for the identification of MZM and to discriminate the topological phases.
tldr: The paper theoretically analyzes finite Rashba nanowires with and without superconducting proximity, deriving transcendental momentum quantization and conditions for zero-energy states that yield distinct conductance signatures for Majorana versus trivial modes.
motivation: Majorana zero modes in semiconductor-superconductor nanowires are a leading platform for topological qubits, but distinguishing true topological zero modes from trivial zero-energy states remains a key experimental challenge.
method: The authors study the canonical low-energy model of a finite Rashba spin-orbit-coupled nanowire, derive exact and approximate wavevector quantization conditions in normal and superconducting phases, and compute linear transport via Andreev reflection and direct transmission.
result: Zero-energy states can appear in both topological and trivial phases, and their conductance lineshapes differ: trivial states show a zero-bias plateau due to negative spin-flip interference, while Majorana zero modes show a peak.
conclusion: The distinct zero-bias conductance lineshape may serve as an experimental signature to identify Majorana zero modes and discriminate topological from trivial phases in Rashba nanowire devices.

title: Leggett–Garg Inequality Violation In Muon G–2 Experiments
authors: Morgan Cassidy And Kun Cheng Brian Batell
abstract: We present the first study of Leggett–Garg inequality (LGI) violation in polarized muon spin precession. We formulate a procedure to reconstruct temporal correlators of the longitudinal muon polarization from measured time-dependent muon decay spectra and apply it to publicly available Fermilab Muon data corresponding to approximately billion muon decays. Using a simplified model of the detector acceptance and efficiency, the LGI is found to be violated with a single-bin significance of , while combining neighboring bins further increases the significance. While our analysis is limited by systematic uncertainties associated with the detector modeling, a dedicated experimental analysis could reduce these uncertainties toward the statistical level, , potentially enabling one of the most precise measurements of temporal quantum correlations.
tldr: The paper reports a first analysis of Leggett–Garg inequality violation in polarized muon spin precession using public Fermilab Muon g−2 data.
motivation: Leggett–Garg inequalities test temporal quantum correlations and macrorealism, and muon spin precession offers a potential high-statistics platform for such foundational tests.
method: The authors reconstruct temporal correlators of longitudinal muon polarization from measured time-dependent muon decay spectra and apply the procedure to public Fermilab Muon g−2 data, using a simplified detector acceptance and efficiency model.
result: The Leggett–Garg inequality is found to be violated with a single-bin significance, and combining neighboring bins increases the significance, though detector-model systematics currently limit the analysis.
conclusion: A dedicated experimental analysis could reduce systematic uncertainties toward the statistical level, potentially enabling one of the most precise measurements of temporal quantum correlations.

title: Rare Event Simulation Of Quantum Error-Correcting Circuits
authors: Carolyn Mayer, Anand Ganti, Uzoma Onunkwo, Tzvetan Metodi, Benjamin Anker, And Jacek Skryzalin
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2237 (2026).

We describe a practical approach for accessing the logical failure rates of quantum error-correcting (QEC) circuits under low physical (component) failure rate regimes. Standard Monte Carlo is often the de facto approach for studying the failure rates of quantum circuits. However, in the study of fault-tolerant error-correcting circuits, the ability to extend this approach to low physical failure rates is limited. In particular, the use of Monte Carlo to access circuits that are relatively large or have high correcting power becomes more difficult as we lower the input failure rates of the individual components (gates) in the circuit. For these reasons, many simulations studying the circuit model go no lower than end-to-end logical failure rates in the [MATH] regime. In this report, we outline an approach that borrows from earlier work by Bravyi and Vargo [6] to the more complex circuit noise model. Earlier works studied both the capacity and phenomenological noise models [6,3,5], but the work is insufficient for generating similar simulations in the circuit-noise model. To the best of our knowledge, our team is the first to develop a full prescription of the rare event simulation by splitting technique for the circuit-based noise model. We have also generated promising results that are confirmed by standard Monte Carlo simulation under an accessible regime. This work shows that we can access noise in the circuit-model prescription of quantum error-correcting code to failure rates below [MATH] regime.

.
tldr: The paper develops a rare-event simulation method for estimating logical failure rates of quantum error-correcting circuits under low circuit-noise regimes.
motivation: Standard Monte Carlo becomes impractical for directly simulating low logical failure rates in fault-tolerant QEC circuits, especially under realistic circuit-level noise.
method: The authors adapt Bravyi-Vargo-style rare-event simulation via splitting to the circuit-noise model and validate it against standard Monte Carlo in an accessible regime.
result: The approach accesses logical failure rates below typical Monte Carlo limits for circuit-based noise and produces results confirmed by standard Monte Carlo where comparisons are feasible.
conclusion: Rare-event simulation is a practical tool for characterizing QEC circuit performance at low physical error rates, extending fault-tolerance studies beyond conventional Monte Carlo reach.

title: Quantum Gouy Phase Singularities In A Propagating Biphoton State
authors: Takumi Jinushi And Hirokazu Kobayashi
abstract: Phase singularities are topological defects around which the phase winds by an integer multiple of . In entangled multiphoton states, they can emerge nonlocally in the joint wavefunction rather than in the field of either subsystem alone. Here we show that the quantum Gouy phase generates nonlocal phase singularities (NPSs) in the two-dimensional longitudinal propagation space of entangled photon pairs. We consider photon pairs produced via spontaneous parametric down-conversion pumped by a Laguerre–Gaussian beam, with the signal and idler photons propagating independently over different longitudinal distances. The accumulated radial-mode-dependent Gouy phases induce destructive interference among biphoton spatial-mode components, producing isolated intensity nulls with quantized phase winding. For a pump with radial mode number , the NPS topological charges have magnitude , whereas their propagation positions and charge signs are governed by the Rayleigh ranges of the pump and phase-matching functions. We further identify the radial-mode structure required for their formation, showing that separable biphoton states cannot support isolated longitudinal NPSs. Our results extend nonlocal singular optics from transverse spatial correlations to longitudinal propagation dynamics and establish propagation distance as a coordinate space for topological structures in entangled photon pairs.
tldr: The paper shows that quantum Gouy phases in a propagating biphoton state can generate nonlocal phase singularities in the longitudinal propagation space of entangled photon pairs.
motivation: Phase singularities in entangled multiphoton states can appear nonlocally in the joint wavefunction, but previous studies have focused mainly on transverse spatial correlations rather than longitudinal propagation dynamics.
method: The authors theoretically analyze photon pairs from spontaneous parametric down-conversion pumped by a Laguerre-Gaussian beam, with signal and idler photons propagating independently over different longitudinal distances, and study the radial-mode-dependent Gouy phases and resulting interference.
result: The accumulated Gouy phases induce destructive interference among biphoton spatial-mode components, producing isolated intensity nulls with quantized phase winding; the topological charge magnitude depends on the pump radial mode number, while positions and signs depend on Rayleigh ranges and phase-matching functions, and separable states cannot support isolated longitudinal nonlocal phase singularities.
conclusion: The work extends nonlocal singular optics to longitudinal propagation dynamics and establishes propagation distance as a coordinate space for topological structures in entangled photon pairs.

title: Variational Perturbation Theory In Open Quantum Systems For Efficient Steady State Computation
authors: André Melo, Gaspard Beugnot, And Fabrizio Minganti
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2246 (2026).

Determining the steady state of an open quantum system is crucial for characterizing quantum devices and studying various physical phenomena. Often, computing a single steady state is insufficient, and it is necessary to explore its dependence on multiple external parameters. In such cases, calculating the steady state independently for each combination of parameters quickly becomes intractable. Perturbation theory (PT) can mitigate this challenge by expanding steady states around reference parameters, minimizing redundant computations across neighboring parameter values. However, PT has two significant limitations: it relies on the pseudo-inverse – a numerically costly operation – and has a limited radius of convergence. In this work, we remove both of these roadblocks. First, we introduce a variational perturbation theory (VPT) and its multipoint generalization that significantly extends the radius of convergence even in the presence of non-analytic effects such as dissipative phase transitions. Then, we develop two numerical strategies that eliminate the need to compute pseudo-inverses. The first relies on a single LU decomposition to efficiently construct the steady state within the convergence region, while the second reformulates VPT as a Krylov space recycling problem and uses preconditioned iterative methods. We benchmark these approaches across various models, demonstrating their broad applicability and significant improvements over standard PT.

.
tldr: The paper introduces variational perturbation theory and numerical strategies to compute steady states of open quantum systems efficiently across parameter ranges.
motivation: Computing steady states independently for many parameter values is intractable, and standard perturbation theory suffers from costly pseudo-inverses and limited convergence radius.
method: The authors develop variational perturbation theory with a multipoint generalization, plus two pseudo-inverse-free numerical schemes: one based on a single LU decomposition and one using Krylov space recycling with preconditioned iterative methods.
result: Benchmarks across several models show extended convergence even near dissipative phase transitions and significant improvements over standard perturbation theory.
conclusion: The approach provides a broadly applicable and efficient tool for steady-state computation and parameter exploration in open quantum systems.

title: Quantum Walks On Arbitrary Spatial Networks With Rydberg Atoms
authors: Gabriel Almeida, Raul Santos, Lara Janiurek, And Yasser Omar
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2235 (2026).

Rydberg atoms provide a highly promising platform for quantum computation, leveraging their strong tunable interactions to encode and manipulate information in the electronic states of individual atoms. Key advantages of Rydberg atoms include scalability, reconfigurable connectivity, and native multi-qubit gates, making them particularly well-suited for addressing complex network problems. These problems can often be framed as graph-based tasks, which can be efficiently addressed using quantum walks. In this work, we propose a general implementation of staggered quantum walks with Rydberg atoms, with a particular focus on spatial networks. We also present an efficient algorithm for constructing the tessellations required for the staggered quantum walk. Finally, we demonstrate that our proposal achieves performance consistent with a quadratic speedup in spatial search algorithms.

.
tldr: The authors propose a general scheme for implementing staggered quantum walks on arbitrary spatial networks using Rydberg-atom arrays, together with an efficient algorithm to construct the required tessellations, and show the scheme is compatible with quadratic speedup in spatial search.
motivation: Rydberg atoms offer scalable, reconfigurable connectivity and native multi-qubit gates, making them attractive for graph-based and network-structured problems that are naturally expressed as quantum walks, but a general implementation for arbitrary spatial networks was missing.
method: They map staggered quantum walks onto Rydberg-atom hardware, exploiting tunable van der Waals interactions to realize the coin and shift operators, and design an efficient algorithm for constructing the tessellations (graph decompositions/clique coverings) required by the walk.
result: The proposal yields a concrete, hardware-feasible construction for arbitrary spatial networks, and analysis shows the resulting spatial search achieves the expected quadratic speedup consistent with theoretical bounds.
conclusion: Rydberg-atom platforms are well suited to implementing quantum walks for network and graph problems, and the tessellation-construction algorithm makes the approach broadly applicable to arbitrary spatial networks.

title: A Counterexample To The Optimality Conjecture In Convex Quantum Channel Optimization
authors: Jianting Yang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2253 (2026).

This paper presents a counterexample to the optimality conjecture for the trace distance based optimal state transformation problem proposed by Coutts et al. [Quantum 5, 448 (2021)]. The conjecture posits that for the trace distance based optimal state transformation problem, applying the sign function to the error matrix uniquely determines a dual certificate for every optimal solution. By constructing a counterexample in 2-dimensional Hilbert spaces, we disprove this conjecture.

.
tldr: This paper constructs a 2-dimensional counterexample disproving the conjectured sign-function dual-certificate characterization for trace-distance-based optimal quantum state transformation.
motivation: Coutts et al. proposed an optimality conjecture for a trace-distance-based state transformation problem, claiming that applying the sign function to the error matrix uniquely determines a dual certificate for every optimal solution.
method: The author explicitly constructs a counterexample in two-dimensional Hilbert spaces to the conjectured dual-certificate condition.
result: The counterexample shows that the sign-function prescription does not always yield a valid unique dual certificate, thereby falsifying the conjecture.
conclusion: The optimality conjecture in convex quantum channel optimization is false in general, so additional conditions or alternative certificate constructions are needed.

title: Quantum Graph Theory By Example
authors: Gian Luca Spitzer And Ion Nechita
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2228 (2026).

Quantum graphs have been introduced by Duan, Severini, and Winter to describe the zero-error behaviour of quantum channels. Since then, quantum graph theory has become a field of study in its own right. A substantial source of difficulty in working with quantum graphs compared to classical graphs stems from the fact that they are no longer discrete objects. This makes it generally difficult to construct insightful, non-trivial examples. We present a collection of non-trivial quantum graphs that can be thought of in discrete terms, and that can be expressed in the diagrammatic formalism introduced by Musto, Reutter, and Verdon. The examples arise as the quantum graphs acted on by increasingly smaller classical matrix groups, and are parametrised by triples of matrices [MATH]. The parametrisation reveals a clean decomposition of quantum graph structure into classical and genuinely quantum components: [MATH] and [MATH] are described by a classical weighted graph called the strange graph, while [MATH] provides a purely quantum contribution with no classical analogue. Based on this model, we give exact formulas or establish bounds for quantum graph parameters, such as the number of connected components, the chromatic number, the independence number, and the clique number. Our results provide the first large, parametric families of quantum graphs for which standard graph parameters can be computed analytically.

.
tldr: The authors construct large parametric families of non-trivial quantum graphs, tied to classical matrix groups and the Musto-Reutter-Verdon diagrammatic formalism, and compute standard graph parameters analytically.
motivation: Quantum graphs, introduced by Duan, Severini and Winter to capture zero-error communication over quantum channels, are continuous (non-discrete) objects, which makes it hard to build insightful examples and to compute invariants.
method: Quantum graphs acted on by successively smaller classical matrix groups are parametrised by triples of matrices, decomposed into a 'strange graph' classical weighted part and a purely quantum component, and analysed in diagrammatic language.
result: Exact formulas or bounds are obtained for the number of connected components, chromatic number, independence number and clique number, giving the first large parametric families of quantum graphs with analytically computable parameters.
conclusion: The parametrisation cleanly separates classical from genuinely quantum graph structure, offering a tractable testbed for quantum graph theory and zero-error channel analysis.

title: Failure Of The Mean-field Hartree Approximation For A Bosonic Many-body System With non-Hermitian Hamiltonian
authors: Matias Ginzburg, Simone Rademacher, And Giacomo de Palma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2244 (2026).

Mean-field Hartree theory is a central tool for reducing many-body dynamics to an effective one-particle evolution. This approximation has been employed when the Hamiltonian governing the many-body dynamics is not Hermitian. Indeed, non-Hermitian Hamiltonians model particle gain/loss or the evolution of open quantum systems between consecutive quantum jumps. Furthermore, the validity of the Hartree approximation for generic non-Hermitian Hamiltonians lies at the basis of a quantum algorithm for nonlinear differential equations. In this work, we show that this approximation can fail. First, we consider the most general bosonic mean-field Hamiltonian with two-body interactions and we prove that, for non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, the Hartree equation does not capture the correct second time derivative of the one-particle marginal state at [MATH] in the thermodynamic limit. Then, we analytically solve a model of [MATH] bosonic qubits with a purely anti-Hermitian Hamiltonian, compute the limit for [MATH] of the one-particle marginal state and show that it does not agree with the solution of the non-Hermitian Hartree equation. We further show that there exists an initial condition such that the exact one-particle marginal state undergoes a finite-time transition to a mixed state, a phenomenon that is completely absent in the case of Hermitian Hamiltonians. Finally, we simulate a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian with real spectrum and show that, also in this case, there are initial conditions for which the Hartree equation does not reproduce the correct one-particle marginal state in the limit [MATH]. Our findings challenge the validity of the mean-field Hartree approximation for non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, and call for additional conditions for the validity of the mean-field regime to model the dynamics of particle gain and loss and the open-system dynamics in bosonic many-body systems.

.
tldr: The paper proves that the mean-field Hartree approximation can fail for bosonic many-body systems governed by non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, with explicit counterexamples showing disagreement between the exact one-particle marginal and the Hartree equation.
motivation: Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians are used to model particle gain/loss and open-system dynamics, and the Hartree approximation underlies some quantum algorithms for nonlinear differential equations, so its validity in this setting is important to establish.
method: The authors analyze the general bosonic mean-field Hamiltonian with two-body interactions, derive a second time-derivative mismatch for the one-particle marginal, solve an anti-Hermitian N-qubit bosonic model analytically, and simulate a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian with real spectrum.
result: They show that the Hartree equation fails to capture the correct second time derivative at t=0, that the exact one-particle marginal disagrees with the Hartree solution in the thermodynamic limit, and that a finite-time transition to a mixed state can occur, absent in Hermitian systems.
conclusion: The findings challenge the validity of the non-Hermitian Hartree approximation for modeling gain/loss and open-system bosonic many-body dynamics, requiring additional conditions for a valid mean-field regime.

title: Coupled Flexural Optomechanical Cavities With Engineered Nanomechanical Interconnects
authors: David Alonso-Tomás, Guillermo Arregui, Bingrui Lu, Sergei Lepeshov, Søren Stobbe And Daniel Navarro-Urrios
abstract: Integrated nanomechanical circuits require compact and predictable ways to read out, confine, and connect mechanical motion across multiple nanoscale elements. This challenge is particularly acute for megahertz flexural modes, whose large mechanical response and nonlinear dynamics are attractive for optomechanics, sensing, and signal processing, but whose extended nature makes local confinement and coupling difficult within dense devices. Here we demonstrate an optomechanical nanobeam platform in which optical transduction and mechanical connectivity are both engineered lithographically. Transverse geometric asymmetry in the photonic-crystal cavity breaks the cancellation that suppresses dispersive coupling to in-plane flexural motion, making these modes optically bright without ancillary structures. In parallel, serpentine mechanical links engineered through their complex band structure are designed as compact mechanical mirrors and experimentally demonstrated as evanescent couplers for MHz flexural waves. In coupled-cavity devices, the normal-mode splitting decays exponentially with the number of serpentine cells, yielding an experimental attenuation constant in quantitative agreement with full-system simulations. Geometry-dependent measurements further show that the coupling can be tuned by the interconnect design and identify regimes where finite-link modes hybridize with the cavity modes, beyond a simple two-resonator picture. These results establish complex-band-engineered mechanical links as calibrated interconnects for scalable optomechanical nanocircuits based on optically addressable MHz flexural resonators.
tldr: The paper demonstrates an optomechanical nanobeam platform with lithographically engineered nanomechanical interconnects for coupling MHz flexural modes between photonic-crystal cavities.
motivation: Integrated nanomechanical circuits need compact, predictable ways to read out, confine, and connect mechanical motion, especially for extended megahertz flexural modes whose confinement and coupling are difficult in dense devices.
method: The authors break transverse geometric symmetry in a photonic-crystal cavity to make in-plane flexural modes optically bright, and use serpentine mechanical links designed via complex band structure as compact mechanical mirrors and evanescent couplers.
result: Coupled-cavity devices show normal-mode splitting that decays exponentially with the number of serpentine cells, with an attenuation constant matching full-system simulations, and coupling tunable by interconnect geometry.
conclusion: Complex-band-engineered mechanical links provide calibrated interconnects for scalable optomechanical nanocircuits based on optically addressable MHz flexural resonators.

title: Enhanced Measurements On Quantum Computers Via The Simultaneous Probing Of Non-commuting Pauli Operators
authors: Rick P. A. Simon, Zheng Shi, Charlie Nation, Andrew Jena, And Luca Dellantonio
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2229 (2026).

Measuring the state of quantum computers is a highly non-trivial task, with implications for virtually all quantum algorithms. A promising avenue is multi-copy schemes, where identical copies of a quantum state are measured jointly so that all Pauli operators within the considered observable can be simultaneously assessed. Here, we present a first implementation of such a two-copy scheme in a measurement protocol. Based on Bayesian statistics, it accurately estimates not only the average of the desired observable but also the error en route. This enables an adaptive shot-allocation algorithm that preferentially samples the most uncertain Pauli terms. In regimes with many non-commuting Pauli operators, this “double'' scheme can outperform the state-of-the-art measurement protocol in minimizing total shots for a given precision. We also numerically confirm the finding in previous theoretical works that the two-copy scheme incurs an overhead due to the square-root relationship between the variance of measured quantities and the number of measurement shots.

.
tldr: The paper implements a two-copy Bayesian measurement scheme for simultaneously estimating non-commuting Pauli operators on quantum computers.
motivation: Measuring quantum states efficiently is central to many quantum algorithms, and multi-copy joint measurements may reduce the number of shots needed for observable estimation.
method: The authors implement a two-copy measurement protocol based on Bayesian statistics and introduce an adaptive shot-allocation algorithm that preferentially samples the most uncertain Pauli terms.
result: In regimes with many non-commuting Pauli operators, the double scheme can outperform state-of-the-art measurement protocols in minimizing total shots for a given precision, while numerically confirming a square-root variance overhead.
conclusion: The work provides a first implementation of a two-copy simultaneous Pauli measurement scheme and demonstrates its potential for improved quantum measurement efficiency, though with known overheads.

title: Proof Of Hiding Conjecture In Gaussian Boson Sampling
authors: Laura Shou, Sarah H. Miller, And Victor Galitski
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2248 (2026).

Gaussian boson sampling (GBS) is a promising protocol for demonstrating quantum computational advantage. One of the key steps in the argument for classical hardness of GBS is the so-called “hiding conjecture'', which asserts that one can “hide'' a complex Gaussian matrix as a submatrix of the symmetric product of Haar unitary submatrices in total variation distance. In this paper, we prove the hiding conjecture for input states with all input modes squeezed, which is a setup that has recently been realized experimentally [10]. In this setting, the hiding conjecture states that a [MATH] submatrix of an [MATH] circular orthogonal ensemble (COE) random matrix can be well-approximated by a complex symmetric Gaussian matrix in total variation distance as [MATH]. This is the first rigorous proof of the hiding property for GBS in the experimentally relevant regime, and puts the argument for hardness of classically simulating GBS with the maximum number of squeezed input modes on a comparable level to that of the conventional boson sampling of [Aaronson and Arkhipov, Theory Comput. 9, 143 (2013)] [1].

.
tldr: The paper rigorously proves the hiding conjecture for Gaussian boson sampling with all input modes squeezed, strengthening the hardness argument for classical simulation.
motivation: Gaussian boson sampling is a leading route to quantum computational advantage, but its classical-hardness argument relies on the unproven hiding conjecture.
method: The authors prove that a submatrix of a circular orthogonal ensemble random matrix can be approximated in total variation distance by a complex symmetric Gaussian matrix in the experimentally relevant all-squeezed-input regime.
result: This gives the first rigorous proof of the hiding property for GBS with the maximum number of squeezed modes, putting its hardness argument on par with conventional boson sampling.
conclusion: The work closes a key theoretical gap in the complexity-theoretic case for Gaussian boson sampling as a quantum advantage demonstration.

title: Optimal Phase Estimation In The Presence Of Correlated Dephasing
authors: Srijon Ghosh, Arkadiusz Kobus, Stanisław Kurdziałek, And Rafał Demkowicz-Dobrzański
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2251 (2026).

We investigate optimal metrological protocols for phase estimation in the presence of correlated dephasing noise, including spin-squeezed state sensing strategies as well as parallel and adaptive protocols optimized using tensor-network-based numerical methods. The results are benchmarked against fundamental bounds obtained either via the latest quantum comb extension method or an optimized classical simulation method. We find that the spin-squeezed states offer practically optimal performance in the regime where phase fluctuations are positively correlated but can be outperformed by tensor-network-optimized strategies for negatively correlated fluctuations.

.
tldr: The paper studies optimal phase-estimation protocols under correlated dephasing, comparing spin-squeezed states with tensor-network-optimized parallel and adaptive strategies against quantum-comb and classical-simulation bounds.
motivation: Correlated dephasing is a realistic noise source in quantum metrology, and it is important to determine which sensing strategies remain optimal when noise correlations are present.
method: The authors analyze spin-squeezed-state sensing and optimize parallel and adaptive protocols numerically using tensor-network methods, benchmarking performance against fundamental bounds from quantum comb extension and optimized classical simulation.
result: Spin-squeezed states are found to be practically optimal for positively correlated phase fluctuations, while tensor-network-optimized strategies can outperform them for negatively correlated fluctuations.
conclusion: The work clarifies the role of noise correlations in phase estimation and identifies regimes where simple squeezed-state strategies suffice versus where more general optimized protocols are needed.

title: Symmetry Defects And Gauging For Quantum States With Matrix Product Unitary Symmetries
authors: Adrián Franco-Rubio, Arkadiusz Bochniak, And J. Ignacio Cirac
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2243 (2026).

In this work, we examine the consequences of the existence of a finite group of matrix product unitary (MPU) symmetries for matrix product states (MPS). We generalize the well-understood picture of onsite unitary symmetries, which give rise to virtual symmetry defects given by insertions of operators in the bonds of the MPS. In the MPU case, we can define analogous defect tensors, this time sitting on lattice sites, that can be created, moved, and fused by local unitary operators. We leverage this formalism to study the gauging of MPU symmetries. We introduce a condition, block independence, under which we can gauge the symmetries by promoting the symmetry defects to gauge degrees of freedom, yielding an MPS of the same bond dimension that supports a local version of the symmetry given by commuting gauge constraints. Whenever block independence does not hold (which happens, in particular, whenever the symmetry representation is anomalous), a modification of our method which we call state-level gauging still gives rise to a locally symmetric MPS by promotion of the symmetry defects, at the expense of producing gauge constraints that do not commute on different sites.

.
tldr: The paper develops a formalism for symmetry defects and gauging of finite matrix product unitary symmetries in matrix product states.
motivation: Onsite unitary symmetries in MPS are well understood via virtual bond defects, but symmetries represented by matrix product unitaries require a site-level defect description. The authors aim to extend this picture and study gauging of such symmetries.
method: They define defect tensors for MPU symmetries that can be created, moved, and fused by local unitaries, and introduce a block-independence condition under which the defects can be promoted to gauge degrees of freedom. They also propose state-level gauging when block independence fails, including anomalous cases.
result: When block independence holds, gauging yields an MPS of the same bond dimension with local commuting gauge constraints. Otherwise, state-level gauging produces a locally symmetric MPS but with noncommuting gauge constraints across sites.
conclusion: The work generalizes symmetry-defect and gauging techniques from onsite symmetries to MPU symmetries in MPS, with implications for anomalous symmetry representations and locally symmetric tensor-network states.

title: Interactive Proofs For Verifying (quantum) Learning And Testing
authors: Matthias C. Caro, Jens Eisert, Marcel Hinsche, Marios Ioannou, Alexander Nietner, And Ryan Sweke
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2239 (2026).

We consider the problem of testing and learning from data in the presence of resource constraints, such as limited memory or weak data access, which place limitations on the efficiency and feasibility of testing or learning. In particular, we ask the following question: Could a resource-constrained learner/tester use interaction with a resource-unconstrained but untrusted party to solve a learning or testing problem more efficiently than they could without such an interaction? In this work, we answer this question both abstractly and for concrete problems, in two complementary ways: For a wide variety of scenarios, we prove that a resource-constrained learner cannot gain any advantage through classical interaction with an untrusted prover. As a special case, we show that for the vast majority of testing and learning problems in which quantum memory is a meaningful resource, a memory-constrained quantum algorithm cannot overcome its limitations via classical communication with a memory-unconstrained quantum prover. In contrast, when quantum communication is allowed, we construct a variety of interactive proof protocols, for specific learning and testing problems, which allow memory-constrained quantum verifiers to gain significant advantages through delegation to untrusted provers. These results highlight both the limitations and potential of delegating learning and testing problems to resource-rich but untrusted third parties.

.
tldr: The paper studies whether memory- or access-constrained learners and testers can benefit from interacting with an untrusted, resource-rich prover, proving impossibility results for classical interaction and constructing advantageous quantum interactive-proof protocols.
motivation: Resource constraints such as limited quantum memory or weak data access restrict what learning and testing algorithms can achieve, motivating the question of whether delegation to a more powerful but untrusted party can circumvent these limits.
method: The authors develop abstract arguments showing that classical interaction with an untrusted prover cannot help a resource-constrained learner for a broad class of problems, and then design concrete interactive proof protocols exploiting quantum communication for specific learning and testing tasks.
result: For a wide range of scenarios, including most problems where quantum memory is a meaningful resource, classical interaction with a memory-unconstrained prover yields no advantage, whereas quantum communication enables significant delegation advantages in explicit protocols.
conclusion: The work delineates the limitations and potential of delegating learning and testing tasks to untrusted third parties, highlighting quantum communication as the essential ingredient for genuine advantage.

title: Re-uploading Quantum Data: A Universal Function Approximator For Quantum Inputs
authors: Hyunho Cha, Daniel K. Park, And Jungwoo Lee
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2256 (2026).

Quantum data re-uploading has proved powerful for classical inputs, where repeatedly encoding features into a small circuit yields universal function approximation. Extending this idea to quantum inputs remains underexplored, as the information contained in a quantum state is not directly accessible in classical form. We propose and analyze a quantum data re-uploading architecture in which a qubit interacts sequentially with fresh copies of an arbitrary input state. The circuit can approximate any bounded continuous function using only one ancilla qubit and single-qubit measurements, provided that sufficiently many copies of the input state and, in general, sufficiently many layers are available. By alternating entangling unitaries with mid-circuit resets of the input register, the architecture realizes a discrete cascade of completely positive and trace-preserving maps, analogous to collision models in open quantum system dynamics. Our framework provides a space-efficient and expressive approach to designing quantum machine learning models that operate directly on quantum data.

.
