tldr: The paper proposes a quantum data re-uploading architecture that approximates bounded continuous functions of quantum inputs using sequential interactions with fresh state copies and single-qubit measurements.
motivation: Quantum data re-uploading is well established for classical inputs, but its extension to quantum inputs is underexplored because quantum information cannot be directly accessed classically.
method: A qubit sequentially interacts with copies of an arbitrary input state, with alternating entangling unitaries and mid-circuit resets, realizing a discrete cascade of completely positive trace-preserving maps analogous to collision models.
result: The architecture can approximate any bounded continuous function using one ancilla qubit and single-qubit measurements, given sufficiently many input copies and layers.
conclusion: The work offers a space-efficient and expressive framework for quantum machine learning directly on quantum data, though its contribution is primarily architectural rather than information-theoretic.

title: Quantum Algorithms For General Nonlinear Dynamics Based On The Carleman Embedding
authors: David Jennings, Kamil Korzekwa, Matteo Lostaglio, Andrew T Sornborger, Yigit Subasi, And Guoming Wang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2233 (2026).

Important nonlinear dynamics, such as those found in plasma and fluid systems, are typically hard to simulate on classical computers. Thus, if fault-tolerant quantum computers could efficiently solve such nonlinear problems, it would be a transformative change for many industries. In a recent breakthrough [Liu et al., PNAS 2021], the first efficient quantum algorithm for solving nonlinear differential equations was constructed, based on a single condition [MATH], where [MATH] characterizes the ratio of nonlinearity to dissipation. This result, however, is limited to the class of purely dissipative systems with negative log-norm, which excludes application to many important problems. In this work, we correct technical issues with this and other prior analysis, and substantially extend the scope of nonlinear dynamical systems that can be efficiently simulated on a quantum computer in a number of ways. Firstly, we extend the existing results from purely dissipative systems to a much broader class of stable systems, and show that every quadratic Lyapunov function for the linearized system corresponds to an independent [MATH]-number criterion for the convergence of the Carleman scheme. Secondly, we extend our stable system results to physically relevant settings where conserved polynomial quantities exist. Finally, we provide extensive results for the class of non-resonant systems. With this, we are able to show that efficient quantum algorithms exist for a much wider class of nonlinear systems than previously known, and prove the BQP-completeness of nonlinear oscillator problems of exponential size. In our analysis, we also obtain several results related to the Poincaré-Dulac theorem and diagonalization of the Carleman matrix, which could be of independent interest.

.
tldr: The authors extend the Carleman-embedding-based quantum algorithm for nonlinear differential equations from purely dissipative systems to a much broader class of stable, conservative, and non-resonant dynamical systems, and prove BQP-completeness of nonlinear oscillator problems.
motivation: Nonlinear dynamics such as plasma and fluid systems are classically hard to simulate; the existing quantum algorithm of Liu et al. only applied to purely dissipative systems with negative log-norm, excluding many important problems.
method: The paper corrects technical issues in prior analyses and generalizes the Carleman linearization framework by deriving Lyapunov-function-based convergence criteria, extending results to systems with conserved polynomial quantities and to non-resonant systems, using results on the Poincaré-Dulac theorem and diagonalization of the Carleman matrix.
result: They show efficient quantum algorithms exist for a substantially wider class of nonlinear systems and establish BQP-completeness of exponentially large nonlinear oscillator problems.
conclusion: The work significantly broadens the class of nonlinear dynamical systems efficiently simulable on fault-tolerant quantum computers, with additional independent results on Carleman matrix diagonalization.

title: Floquet-ADAPT-VQE: A Quantum Algorithm To Simulate Non-Equilibrium Physics In Periodically Driven Systems
authors: Abhishek Kumar, Karunya Shirali, Nicholas J. Mayhall, Sophia E. Economou, And Edwin Barnes
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2247 (2026).

Periodically driven quantum systems exhibit many fascinating phenomena absent in equilibrium systems, but their simulation is more challenging than that of static systems. Consequently, quantum simulation of these systems offers greater opportunity for achieving quantum advantage. To build the foundation for simulating time-periodic Hamiltonians, we utilize the Floquet-Hilbert space formalism to transform the Hamiltonian into a time-independent form and provide its Pauli decomposition. Within this formalism, we develop a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm, Floquet-ADAPT-VQE, that produces three key quantities that govern periodically driven quantum dynamics: the quasienergy, the associated Floquet eigenstates, and expectation values of observables with respect to these eigenstates. The latter is achieved by applying a fixed-depth quantum circuit to an initial Floquet eigenstate—an efficient construction made possible by the Floquet-Hilbert space formalism. We also identify a suitable auxiliary initial state whose squared Floquet energy is independent of the number of auxiliary qubits as well as the driving frequency, which leads to better convergence with fewer ADAPT iterations. We demonstrate our algorithm by performing numerical simulations on a periodically driven XYZ model with a magnetic field. We also explore potential applications of our algorithm for studying various non-equilibrium phenomena in periodically driven systems.

.
tldr: Introduces Floquet-ADAPT-VQE, a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for computing quasienergies, Floquet eigenstates, and observables in periodically driven quantum systems.
motivation: Periodically driven quantum systems exhibit rich non-equilibrium phenomena but are more challenging to simulate than static systems, motivating specialized quantum algorithms.
method: The authors use the Floquet-Hilbert space formalism to map a time-periodic Hamiltonian to a time-independent form with a Pauli decomposition, then develop an ADAPT-VQE variant that variationally prepares Floquet eigenstates and evaluates observables.
result: Numerical simulations on a periodically driven XYZ model with a magnetic field demonstrate the algorithm, and a suitable auxiliary initial state is identified whose squared Floquet energy is independent of auxiliary-qubit number and driving frequency, improving convergence.
conclusion: The work provides a foundation for quantum simulation of time-periodic Hamiltonians and suggests applications to studying non-equilibrium phenomena in driven systems.

title: Sampled-Based Guided Quantum Walk: Non-variational Quantum Algorithm For Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Ugo Nzongani, Dylan Laplace Mermoud, Giuseppe Di Molfetta, And Andrea Simonetto
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2234 (2026).

We introduce SamBa-GQW, a novel quantum algorithm for solving binary combinatorial optimization problems of arbitrary degree with no use of any classical optimizer. The algorithm is based on a continuous-time quantum walk on the solution space represented as a graph. The walker explores the solution space to find its way to vertices that minimize the cost function of the optimization problem. The key novelty of our algorithm is an offline classical sampling protocol that gives information about the spectrum of the problem Hamiltonian. Then, the extracted information is used to guide the walker to high quality solutions via a quantum walk with a time-dependent hopping rate. We investigate the performance of SamBa-GQW on several quadratic problems, namely MaxCut, maximum independent set, portfolio optimization, and higher-order polynomial problems such as LABS, MAX-[MATH]-SAT and a quartic reformulation of the travelling salesperson problem. We empirically demonstrate that SamBa-GQW finds high quality approximate solutions on problems up to a size of [MATH] qubits by only sampling poly([MATH]) states among [MATH] possible decisions. Furthermore, SamBa-GQW compares in par with classically optimized variational approaches, such as the variational guided quantum walk and QAOA (the latter when run on deep circuits). This places Samba-GQW as a promising heuristic to tackle combinatorial problems beyond the NISQ regime.

.
tldr: SamBa-GQW is a non-variational quantum algorithm that solves binary combinatorial optimization problems by running a continuous-time quantum walk on the solution-space graph, with hopping rates guided by classically sampled spectral information from the problem Hamiltonian.
motivation: Variational quantum heuristics such as QAOA and variational guided quantum walks require expensive classical outer-loop optimization, which is impractical beyond the NISQ regime; the authors seek a fully non-variational alternative that still reaches high-quality solutions.
method: An offline classical sampling protocol extracts information about the spectrum of the problem Hamiltonian, which is then used to define a time-dependent hopping rate for a continuous-time quantum walk over the solution-space graph, steering the walker toward low-cost vertices without any classical optimizer.
result: Empirical tests on MaxCut, maximum independent set, portfolio optimization, LABS, MAX-k-SAT and a quartic TSP reformulation show high-quality approximate solutions for problems up to hundreds of qubits while sampling only poly(n) states, competitive with classically optimized variational guided quantum walks and deep-circuit QAOA.
conclusion: SamBa-GQW is presented as a promising non-variational heuristic for combinatorial optimization that may scale to regimes beyond NISQ, though the evidence is empirical and heuristic in nature.

title: Model Predictive Quantum Control: A Modular Approach For Efficient And Robust Quantum Optimal Control
authors: Eya Guizani And Julian Berberich
abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) is one of the most successful modern control methods. It relies on repeatedly solving a finite-horizon optimal control problem and applying the beginning piece of the optimal input. In this paper, we develop a modular framework for improving efficiency and robustness of quantum optimal control (QOC) via MPC. We first provide a tutorial introduction to basic concepts of MPC from a QOC perspective. We then present multiple MPC schemes, ranging from simple approaches to more sophisticated schemes which admit stability guarantees. This yields a modular framework which can be used 1) to improve efficiency of open-loop QOC and 2) to improve robustness of closed-loop quantum control by incorporating feedback. We demonstrate these benefits with numerical results, where we benchmark the proposed methods against competing approaches.
tldr: The paper develops a modular model predictive control framework to improve the efficiency and robustness of quantum optimal control.
motivation: Quantum optimal control often suffers from computational inefficiency and sensitivity to disturbances, motivating control-theoretic methods that can reuse open-loop solutions and incorporate feedback.
method: The authors give a tutorial-style introduction to model predictive control from a quantum control perspective and propose several MPC schemes, including variants with stability guarantees, for open-loop efficiency and closed-loop robustness.
result: Numerical benchmarks show that the proposed MPC schemes can improve efficiency and robustness relative to competing quantum optimal control approaches.
conclusion: Model predictive control offers a modular and practical route to more efficient and robust quantum control, though the work is control-theoretic rather than aligned with the listed quantum information research directions.

title: Topological Tricritical Ising Universality Class In One Dimension
authors: Hai-Qing Lin And Xue-Jia Yu Sheng Yang
abstract: Quantum critical points can host symmetry-protected topological (SPT) edge modes even when the bulk is gapless, giving rise to symmetry-enriched universality classes beyond the conventional Landau–Ginzburg–Wilson paradigm. Here we show that the tricritical Ising (TCI) critical point—described by a paradigmatic conformal field theory (CFT) with emergent supersymmetry—admits a topologically nontrivial, symmetry-enriched realization, which we term the topological TCI. We construct this critical point in the cluster O’Brien–Fendley (OF) spin chain by applying an SPT entangler to the original OF model. The two realizations therefore share the same bulk TCI CFT. Under open boundary conditions, however, the original model exhibits the free conformal boundary condition, whereas the cluster model exhibits a spontaneously fixed boundary condition: an infinitesimal boundary field can select one of the fixed boundary states, yielding spontaneous boundary magnetization. We further show that symmetry enrichment and boundary renormalization-group flow provide two routes to the spontaneously fixed boundary condition. Whereas the free and spontaneously fixed boundary conditions of the original model can be interconverted by tuning a symmetry-preserving boundary term, no such conversion occurs for the cluster model along the boundary deformations studied here, even in the strong-deformation limit. Although they share the same conventional boundary CFT (BCFT) data, including the boundary operator content and boundary -function, the two realizations of the spontaneously fixed boundary condition are distinguished by different time-reversal charges of the disorder field, which impose different symmetry constraints on the allowed boundary conditions under symmetry-preserving boundary deformations. For the tested symmetry-preserving boundary perturbations that lift the exact twofold degeneracy, the finite-size energy splitting is numerically consistent with exponential decay over accessible system sizes, in stark contrast to the algebraic splitting at the symmetry-enriched Ising critical point of the cluster Ising spin chain. We also find that the topological TCI realization persists along a critical line in a two-parameter phase diagram. These results establish a symmetry-enriched TCI universality class and uncover boundary distinctions invisible to conventional BCFT data.
tldr: The paper constructs a symmetry-enriched topological tricritical Ising critical point in a cluster O’Brien–Fendley spin chain and distinguishes boundary phases via boundary CFT and time-reversal charges.
motivation: Quantum critical points with SPT edge modes can realize symmetry-enriched universality classes beyond conventional Landau–Ginzburg–Wilson paradigms, motivating the search for topologically nontrivial realizations of known CFTs.
method: An SPT entangler is applied to the original O’Brien–Fendley model to construct the topological TCI, followed by boundary CFT analysis, symmetry arguments, and numerical finite-size scaling of boundary energy splittings.
result: The cluster model shares the bulk TCI CFT but exhibits a spontaneously fixed boundary condition with distinct time-reversal charge assignments, leading to exponential rather than algebraic finite-size splitting under tested symmetry-preserving perturbations.
conclusion: The results establish a symmetry-enriched TCI universality class and reveal boundary distinctions invisible to conventional BCFT data, with the topological realization persisting along a critical line.

title: A Symmetry-Enabled Direct Quantum Protocol For Many-Body Green’s Functions
authors: Changhao Yi And Cunlu Zhou
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2245 (2026).

We present a symmetry-enabled direct quantum protocol for computing many-body Green's functions, a central tool for studying strongly correlated quantum systems. Our protocol relies only on native time evolution and straightforward measurements available on current hardware platforms. By exploiting parity symmetry—satisfied by a broad class of Hamiltonians in condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry, including the Fermi–Hubbard and Heisenberg models—we introduce a tailored quench spectroscopy scheme that recovers both the real and imaginary parts of two-point time correlators, from which Green's functions can be reconstructed via efficient classical signal processing. We further develop a tailored symmetric quantum Gibbs sampler that prepares parity-resolved (symmetric and antisymmetric) thermal states, enabling finite-temperature extensions within the same framework. Finally, we show that the same symmetry-based measurement primitive extends naturally to out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs). Our results provide a practical route to estimating symmetry-resolved dynamical correlators on near-term and early fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

.
tldr: The paper proposes a symmetry-enabled quantum protocol for computing many-body Green's functions and related dynamical correlators using native time evolution and simple measurements.
motivation: Many-body Green's functions are essential for strongly correlated systems, but direct quantum computation of real and imaginary time correlators remains challenging on near-term hardware.
method: The authors exploit parity symmetry to design a tailored quench spectroscopy scheme, reconstructing two-point correlators via classical signal processing, and introduce a symmetric quantum Gibbs sampler for finite-temperature states; the measurement primitive also extends to OTOCs.
result: The protocol recovers both real and imaginary parts of two-point time correlators and enables parity-resolved thermal states, with extensions to out-of-time-ordered correlators.
conclusion: This provides a practical route for symmetry-resolved dynamical correlator estimation on near-term and early fault-tolerant quantum devices.

title: Towards Local And Compositional Measurements In Quantum Field Theory
authors: Robert Oeckl And Adamantia Zampeli
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2232 (2026).

A universal framework for the joint measurement of multiple localized observables in quantum field theory satisfying spacetime locality and compositionality is still lacking. We present an approach to the problem that is based on the one hand on the positive formalism, an axiomatic framework, where it is clear from the outset that we satisfy locality and compositionality, while also having a consistent probabilistic interpretation. On the other hand, the approach is based on standard tools from quantum field theory, in particular the path integral and the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism. After an overview of the conceptual foundations we introduce the modulus-square construction as a formalization of the measurement process for the expectation value of an important class of observables including quadratic observables. We show that this construction has many of the desired properties, including positivity, locality, single measurement recovery and compositionality. We introduce a renormalization scheme for the measurement of quadratic observables that also satisfies compositionality, in contrast to previous renormalization schemes. We discuss relativistic causality, confirming that measurements in our scheme are indeed localized in the spacetime regions where the underlying observables have support.

.
tldr: The paper proposes a positive-formalism and path-integral/Schwinger-Keldysh approach to define local and compositional measurements of localized observables in quantum field theory.
motivation: A universal framework for joint measurement of multiple localized observables in QFT satisfying spacetime locality and compositionality is still lacking.
method: The authors combine the positive formalism, an axiomatic probabilistic framework, with standard QFT tools such as the path integral and Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, introducing a modulus-square construction for measurement.
result: They show the construction has positivity, locality, single-measurement recovery, and compositionality, and introduce a compositional renormalization scheme for quadratic observables while confirming relativistic causality/localization.
conclusion: The work provides foundational progress on local and compositional measurements in QFT, but it does not align directly with the listed quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid-systems research directions.

title: A Comprehensive Benchmark Of An Ising Machine On The Max-Cut Problem
authors: Salwa Shaglel, Markus Kirsch, Marten Winkler, Christian Münch, Stefan Walter, Fritz Schinkel And Martin Kliesch
abstract: Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) formulations of combinatorial optimization problems allow for solving them using various quantum heuristics. While large-scale quantum computations are currently still out of reach, we can already numerically test such QUBO formulations on a perhaps surprisingly large scale. In this work, we benchmark Fujitsu’s Digital Annealer (DA) on the Max-Cut problem, which captures the main complexity of the QUBO problem. We make a comprehensive benchmark against leading other heuristic algorithms on graphs with up to 53,000 variables by focusing on the wall-clock time. Moreover, we compare the DA performance against published performance results of the D-Wave hybrid quantum–classical annealer and the recently proposed QIS3 heuristic. Based on performance statistics for over 2000 graphs from the MQLib, we find that the DA yields competitive results. We hope that this benchmark demonstrates the extent to which large QUBO instances can be heuristically solved today, yielding consistent results across different solvers.
tldr: The paper benchmarks Fujitsu's Digital Annealer against other heuristics on large Max-Cut/QUBO instances, finding competitive wall-clock performance.
motivation: QUBO formulations enable quantum and quantum-inspired heuristics for combinatorial optimization, but large-scale quantum computation is not yet available, so benchmarking current heuristic solvers is practically important.
method: The authors evaluate the Digital Annealer on over 2,000 MQLib graphs with up to 53,000 variables, comparing wall-clock time and solution quality against leading classical heuristics and published D-Wave hybrid and QIS3 results.
result: The Digital Annealer achieves competitive performance across the benchmark suite, demonstrating that large QUBO instances can be solved effectively by today's heuristic hardware.
conclusion: The study provides a comprehensive empirical benchmark of an Ising-machine heuristic for Max-Cut, but it is an applied optimization/benchmarking paper rather than a contribution to quantum information theory, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Field-quadrature Perspective On Strong-field Ionization With Squeezed Light
authors: Jianmin Yuan And Xu Wang Haoyu Liu
abstract: Bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) has emerged as a macroscopic nonclassical light source capable of driving strong-field processes. Yet its broad, long-tailed photon-number distribution bears little resemblance to the narrow poissonian distribution of a coherent field, obscuring how the corresponding strong-field responses are connected. We show that field-quadrature space supplies the missing continuous description: coherent, squeezed coherent, and BSV states are Gaussian wave packets distinguished only by their centers and widths. This representation provides a unified framework for tracing the coherent-to-BSV transition at fixed mean photon number and for analyzing both ionization yields and photoelectron spectra. Crucially, BSV is a symmetry-protected endpoint in quadrature space. Near the BSV limit, we identify a simple scaling law of the ionization response associated with a residual coherent component. We show that this scaling arises from parity-induced stationarity with respect to the Gaussian center, together with the accompanying width variation near the BSV limit. The result provides a symmetry-based criterion for approaching the BSV regime and a potential probe of a mode-matched coherent displacement through the strong-field response itself.
tldr: The paper analyzes strong-field ionization driven by bright squeezed vacuum using a field-quadrature Gaussian-state framework, identifying a symmetry-protected scaling law near the BSV limit.
motivation: BSV has a broad photon-number distribution unlike coherent light, making it unclear how strong-field ionization responses connect across coherent-to-squeezed regimes.
method: The authors represent coherent, squeezed coherent, and BSV states as Gaussian wave packets in field-quadrature space and use this to compute ionization yields and photoelectron spectra at fixed mean photon number.
result: They find a simple scaling law for the ionization response near the BSV limit, arising from parity-induced stationarity in the Gaussian center and accompanying width variation.
conclusion: Field-quadrature space provides a unified description of strong-field ionization with nonclassical light and suggests a symmetry-based probe of mode-matched coherent displacement.

title: From Optical Gain To Lasing With Colloidal Nanocrystals
authors: Ivo Tanghe, Zeger Hens, Dries van Thourhout And Pieter Geiregat
abstract: Colloidal semiconductor nanocrystals (NCs) are widely explored as optical gain materials, and throughout over 20 years of research their performance is evaluated through transient absorption spectroscopy (TAS) using parameters such as gain magnitude, lifetime, and threshold. In this work, we discuss some of the literature values reported and couple that to different gain mechanisms. Next, we take a closer look at how these actually relate to the physical parameters that govern lasing, as described by the semiconductor laser rate equations, and found some discrepancy with what is usually reported and what is necessary. We introduce a new analytical framework that connects TAS data to two new fundamental quantities: the stimulated emission rate, representing the intrinsic light–matter interaction speed, and the carrier recombination time, which determines the competing nonradiative loss channel. Together with the already typically reported transparency density, these parameters enable direct prediction of key laser characteristics, like threshold behavior for both femto- and quasi-CW excitation, without requiring full device fabrication. Applying this methodology to a range of colloidal NC systems, we demonstrate that their intrinsic gain performance approaches that of epitaxially grown quantum wells. Analysis of colloidal NC laser literature data further confirms the consistency and predictive power of this approach. This work establishes a unified basis for interpreting ultrafast spectroscopy of NCs and provides a more quantitative route to benchmarking emerging materials for integrated laser technologies.
tldr: The paper introduces an analytical framework linking transient absorption spectroscopy of colloidal nanocrystals to fundamental laser gain parameters such as stimulated emission rate, carrier recombination time, and transparency density.
motivation: Colloidal semiconductor nanocrystals are widely studied as optical gain materials, but their lasing potential is often assessed using TAS metrics that may not directly map onto the physical parameters governing lasing.
method: The authors review literature gain values and mechanisms, connect TAS data to semiconductor laser rate equations, and define two new quantities—stimulated emission rate and carrier recombination time—to predict laser threshold behavior without device fabrication.
result: Applying the framework to various colloidal nanocrystal systems shows that their intrinsic gain performance approaches that of epitaxial quantum wells, and literature data confirm the consistency and predictive power of the approach.
conclusion: The work provides a unified basis for interpreting ultrafast spectroscopy of nanocrystals and a more quantitative route for benchmarking emerging materials for integrated laser technologies.

title: Zak Phase And Bulk-boundary Correspondence In A Generalized Dirac–Kronig–Penney Model
authors: Domenico Monaco And Gabriele Peluso Giuliano Angelone
abstract: We investigate the topological properties of a generalized Dirac–Kronig–Penney model, a continuum one-dimensional model for a relativistic quantum chain. By tuning the coupling parameters this model can accommodate five Altland–Zirnbauer–Cartan symmetry classes, three of which (AIII, BDI and D) support non-trivial topological phases in dimension one. We characterize analytically the spectral properties of the Hamiltonian in terms of a spectral function, and numerically compute the Zak phase to probe the bulk topological content of the insulating phases. Our findings reveal that, while the Zak phase is quantized in classes AIII and BDI, it exhibits non-quantized values in class D, challenging its traditional role as a topological marker in continuum settings. We also discuss the bulk-boundary correspondence for a truncated version of the chain, analyzing how the emergence of edge states depends on both the truncation position and the boundary conditions. In classes AIII and BDI, we find that the Zak phase effectively detects edge states as a relative boundary topological index, although the correspondence is highly sensitive to the parameters characterizing the truncation.
tldr: The paper analyzes Zak phase and bulk-boundary correspondence in a generalized one-dimensional Dirac–Kronig–Penney model across several Altland–Zirnbauer symmetry classes.
motivation: The authors aim to clarify how the Zak phase behaves as a topological marker in continuum one-dimensional topological phases and how robustly it predicts edge states under truncation.
method: They analytically characterize the spectrum via a spectral function and numerically compute the Zak phase for insulating phases in classes AIII, BDI, and D, then study a truncated chain with varying boundary conditions.
result: The Zak phase is quantized in classes AIII and BDI but non-quantized in class D, and edge-state detection via the Zak phase is highly sensitive to truncation parameters and boundary conditions.
conclusion: The work challenges the standard role of the Zak phase as a bulk topological invariant in continuum settings and highlights sensitivity of bulk-boundary correspondence to truncation details.

title: Incoherent Diffraction Imaging With A Pseudo-thermal Light Source
authors: Pablo San Miguel Claveria, Peer Biesterfeld, Sebastião Antunes, Matilde Fernandes, Matilde Garcia, Matilde Nunes, Lucas Ansia Fernandez, Gareth O Williams, Sven Froehlich, David Theidel, Philip Mosel, Ihsan Fsaifes, Andrea Trabattoni, Marco Piccardo, Jean-Christophe Chanteloup, Milutin Kovacev, Hamed Merdji And Marta Fajardo
abstract: Incoherent diffraction imaging—IDI—is a lensless imaging technique that has been recently proposed to exploit the partial coherence of incoherently scattered light to retrieve structural information from the scattering centers. Similar to the stellar intensity interferometry of Hanbury Brown and Twiss, the signal builds up on the second-order spatial correlations of the emitted light. The complex spatial distribution of the target is thereby encoded in the spatial intensity fluctuations of the scattered light. The first experimental realizations of this imaging technique have been realized using the fluorescence excited by an ultra-short x-ray pulse at free electron laser (FEL) facilities. Here, we propose an alternative setup based on a table-top pseudo-thermal light source that works as an optical emulator of the FEL experiment. This setup allows us to explore IDI under a wide range of physically relevant conditions as well as to benchmark numerical and analytical models currently used to determine the imaging capabilities of this technique.
tldr: The paper proposes and benchmarks incoherent diffraction imaging using a table-top pseudo-thermal light source as an optical emulator of X-ray free-electron-laser experiments.
motivation: Incoherent diffraction imaging exploits second-order spatial correlations of incoherently scattered light to recover structural information, but existing demonstrations rely on X-ray FEL facilities and need broader benchmarking.
method: The authors use a table-top pseudo-thermal light source to emulate FEL-based incoherent diffraction imaging and compare experimental results with numerical and analytical models.
result: The setup enables exploration of incoherent diffraction imaging under varied physically relevant conditions and provides a testbed for assessing imaging capabilities and model predictions.
conclusion: A pseudo-thermal source can serve as a flexible optical emulator for developing and validating incoherent diffraction imaging techniques relevant to X-ray FEL experiments.

title: Collective Excitations In Quantum Gravity Condensates
authors: Adrià Delhom And Daniele Oriti Andrea Calcinari
abstract: A central open problem in quantum gravity is to understand how continuum spacetime emerges from quantum-geometric degrees of freedom in a background-independent setting. A many-body perspective suggests that spacetime emerges as a hydrodynamic phase of many atoms of quantum geometry. This idea underlies several approaches to quantum gravity, and it has been explicitly realised in the group field theory formalism. However, quantum fluctuations beyond the mean-field regime remain largely unexplored. We fill this gap by importing Bogolyubov theory to quantum gravity condensates, showing that leading beyond-mean-field effects manifest as collective excitations, in direct analogy with phonons in laboratory Bose–Einstein condensates. We implement the construction in a tractable group field theory model, where condensates of quantum-geometric atoms reproduce nonsingular expanding cosmologies, and derive the leading beyond-mean-field corrections to the emergent Friedmann dynamics. These results identify a new class of quantum-gravity excitations and establish a controlled bridge between microscopic quantum-gravitational dynamics, many-body collective phenomena, and signatures of spacetime emergence.
tldr: The paper applies Bogolyubov theory to group field theory quantum gravity condensates to study beyond-mean-field collective excitations and their corrections to emergent Friedmann dynamics.
motivation: Understanding how continuum spacetime emerges from microscopic quantum-geometric degrees of freedom remains a central open problem in quantum gravity, and beyond-mean-field fluctuations in quantum gravity condensates are largely unexplored.
method: The authors import Bogolyubov theory from laboratory Bose-Einstein condensates into a tractable group field theory model of quantum-geometric atoms and derive leading beyond-mean-field corrections to the emergent cosmological dynamics.
result: They identify a new class of quantum-gravity collective excitations analogous to phonons and obtain corrections to the emergent Friedmann equations in nonsingular expanding cosmologies.
conclusion: The work establishes a controlled bridge between microscopic quantum-gravitational dynamics, many-body collective phenomena, and spacetime emergence, but it is not directly aligned with quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Parallel Adaptive Reweighting Importance Sampling For Bayesian Astrophysics
authors: Miaoxin Liu And Alvin J K Chua
abstract: Efficient sampling from high-dimensional, multi-modal posteriors is a central challenge in Bayesian inference across the physical sciences. Gravitational-wave (GW) astronomy, where likelihood evaluations are computationally expensive and posteriors are complex, is one application motivating this work. Popular families of methods like Markov-chain Monte Carlo, Snested sampling, and importance sampling (IS) all rely on proposal distributions to guide exploration. Because prior knowledge of the target is often limited, practitioners can adopt adaptive proposals that iteratively refine themselves using information gained from previously drawn samples. Traditional adaptive strategies, however, struggle in high-dimensional multi-modal settings: complex, non-linear correlations are hard to capture, and hyperparameters typically require tedious, problem-specific tuning. To address these issues, we introduce parallel adaptive reweighting IS (PARIS; descriptively, ‘seed sampling’). PARIS models its proposal as a Gaussian mixture whose component centers are the existing samples and whose component weights match the current importance weights. New draws from the proposal therefore concentrate around high-weight regions, while candidate points in unexplored areas receive intentionally inflated weights. As the algorithm continuously reweights all samples up to the latest proposal, any initial over-weighting self-corrects once additional neighbor samples are collected. To enable rapid reweighting, we present an efficient update scheme and evaluate PARIS on illustrative toy problems and more realistic GW parameter estimation tasks. PARIS achieves accurate posterior reconstruction and evidence estimation with substantially fewer function evaluations than competing approaches, highlighting its promise for widespread use in astrophysical data analysis.
tldr: The paper introduces PARIS, a parallel adaptive reweighting importance-sampling algorithm for efficient Bayesian posterior and evidence estimation in high-dimensional multimodal problems, with application to gravitational-wave astrophysics.
motivation: Sampling complex multimodal posteriors is costly in gravitational-wave astronomy and other physical sciences, and existing adaptive proposal methods struggle with high dimensionality, correlations, and hyperparameter tuning.
method: PARIS models the proposal as a Gaussian mixture centered on existing samples with weights matching current importance weights, and uses an efficient update scheme to continuously reweight all samples as the proposal evolves.
result: The method achieves accurate posterior reconstruction and evidence estimation with substantially fewer likelihood evaluations than competing approaches on toy problems and realistic gravitational-wave parameter-estimation tasks.
conclusion: PARIS is presented as a promising practical sampling method for astrophysical data analysis, though it is not directly connected to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: From Band Reconstruction To Bogoliubov Dispersion: How Dz 2-band Enhances Iron-based Superconductivity
authors: Jingming Yan, Shendong Su, Guihao Jia, Yucong Peng, Xuanyu Long, Zheng Liu, Pei Ouyang, Qi-Kun Xue And Wei Li
abstract: Conventional understanding of iron-based superconductivity is usually established based on electronic bands at the Fermi level, leaving deeper bands overlooked as potential factor. Here, we expand this view by demonstrating that a deep-lying dz2 band below the Fermi level can be employed to enhance the superconducting paring strength. By using scanning tunneling microscope to mechanically change the crystal lattice of an iron-based superconductor, we observe an upward shift of the deep-lying dz2 band related feature, leading to hybridization with the primary superconducting bands at the Fermi level. We visualize the novel evidence of this band hybridization and resulting enhanced superconducting gap through quasiparticle interference imaging, providing conclusive evidence that engineering such correlations between deep and pairing-active bands is a potent mechanism for amplifying the superconducting gap. This work refines the conventional view of pairing-relevant electronic structures and establishes band hybridization as an effective way to optimize superconducting materials.
tldr: The paper uses STM to show that a deep-lying dz2 band in an iron-based superconductor can hybridize with Fermi-level bands and enhance the superconducting gap.
motivation: Conventional studies of iron-based superconductivity focus on bands at the Fermi level, overlooking deeper bands as potential contributors to pairing.
method: The authors mechanically tune the crystal lattice of an iron-based superconductor with a scanning tunneling microscope and use quasiparticle interference imaging to visualize band hybridization.
result: They observe an upward shift of a deep dz2 band feature, its hybridization with primary superconducting bands, and a resulting enhancement of the superconducting gap.
conclusion: Engineering correlations between deep and pairing-active bands via band hybridization is proposed as an effective route to amplify superconducting pairing.

title: Small-angle Solution Scattering: From Fundamental Theory To Practical Approximations
authors: Jan Skov Pedersen And Jochen S Hub Kristian Lytje
abstract: Small-angle scattering (SAS) with x-rays and neutrons is widely used in structural biology, soft matter, and colloidal science to probe molecular structures in solution. SAS rests on a single physical principle: wave interference from a distribution of scatterers. Yet the theoretical foundations of SAS are spread across the literature, often based on differing notation, definitions, and implicit assumptions. We present the theory of SAS in solution starting from the first Born approximation as a continuous derivation, spanning the scattering of a single electron to the observed intensity of a molecular solution and its comparison with atomistic structural models. The derivation is explicit throughout—approximations, averaging procedures, and algebraic manipulations are stated rather than assumed—and the resulting expressions are independent of the probe (x-ray or neutron) and apply to both rigid and flexible molecules. The framework resolves several ambiguities in the current literature, notably the role of background subtraction as a theoretical rather than a purely experimental operation and the role of boundary cross-terms in justifying that subtraction. A central result is that analytical scattering calculations and approaches based on explicit-solvent molecular dynamics, typically treated as distinct traditions, are realizations of the common theoretical framework derived here. As the precision and reproducibility of SAS data continue to increase, this comprehensive framework provides a basis for integrating theory, simulation, and experiment in future developments of SAS.
tldr: A comprehensive, self-contained derivation of small-angle X-ray and neutron solution scattering theory, from the first Born approximation to comparison with atomistic structural models.
motivation: The theoretical foundations of small-angle scattering are scattered across the literature with inconsistent notation, definitions, and implicit assumptions, creating ambiguities that hinder rigorous integration of theory, simulation, and experiment.
method: The authors build a continuous, explicit derivation starting from the first Born approximation, covering scattering from a single electron through to the observed intensity of a molecular solution, making all approximations, averaging procedures, and algebraic steps explicit and probe-independent.
result: The framework resolves literature ambiguities—notably background subtraction as a theoretical rather than purely experimental operation and the role of boundary cross-terms—and shows that analytical scattering calculations and explicit-solvent molecular dynamics approaches are two realizations of one common theoretical framework.
conclusion: The unified framework provides a foundation for integrating theory, simulation, and experiment as SAS data precision and reproducibility continue to improve.

title: Spatiotemporal Mode-locked Fiber Lasers: Multidimensional Soliton Dynamics Revealed By Real-time Measurement
authors: Yi Zhou, Can Li, Zhuopeng Han, Kun Jin, Bo Ren, Zhenqiang Tang, Tao Wang, Zhiwen He, Jinyong Leng And Pu Zhou
abstract: Spatiotemporal mode-locked multimode fiber lasers have emerged as a promising platform for investigating nonlinear multidimensional physics, with prospective applications ranging from high-energy pulse generation and precise metrology to nonlinear microscopy. The fundamental mechanism governing ultrashort pulse formation in nonlinear multimode resonators, which can be interpreted as multidimensional dissipative solitons (MDSs), lies in spatiotemporal mode-locking (STML), which achieves synchronous locking of both temporal and spatial modes. In this review, the general principles of STML are initially elaborated, with a focus on MDS dynamics under real-time measurement. Subsequently, we summarize the operational principles of versatile real-time measurement techniques and recent advancements in characterizing the ultrafast transient MDS dynamics of STML lasers, including spatial mode switching, optical rogue waves, mode-locking buildup process, three-dimensional soliton molecules, soliton explosions, and breathing multimode solitons. Finally, we outline some perspectives on how real-time measurement methods could advance the study of multidimensional soliton dynamics in STML in the near future.
tldr: This review covers spatiotemporal mode-locking in multimode fiber lasers and real-time measurement of multidimensional dissipative soliton dynamics.
motivation: Multimode fiber lasers provide a platform for nonlinear multidimensional physics, but understanding ultrashort pulse formation requires characterizing complex spatiotemporal soliton dynamics.
method: The review explains general STML principles, surveys real-time measurement techniques, and summarizes recent experimental characterizations of transient MDS dynamics.
result: It discusses phenomena including spatial mode switching, optical rogue waves, mode-locking buildup, three-dimensional soliton molecules, soliton explosions, and breathing multimode solitons.
conclusion: The paper outlines future perspectives on using real-time measurement to advance the study of multidimensional soliton dynamics in STML lasers.

title: Nonflow Subtraction Beyond Two-particle Correlations
authors: Zaining Wang, Jiangyong Jia, Jinhui Chen, Shengli Huang, Chunjian Zhang And Zhengxi Yan
abstract: Establishing collective flow in small collision systems is a crucial and necessary condition for pinning down the minimum conditions for quark-gluon plasma formation. In two-particle correlations, nonflow has been subtracted with good control, pushing the reach of flow measurements down to very small event particle multiplicity . However, the multi-particle nature of collectivity has not been established in the same regime, because the residual nonflow surviving the subevent procedure in multi-particle cumulants has never been quantified. We develop a general nonflow subtraction framework for -particle cumulants, built around the approximate scaling of nonflow in the independent-source picture. Correlators containing serve as nonflow-dominated estimators, since the -integrated dipolar flow is expected to be small. Using hijing as a controlled nonflow-only environment, we test the subtraction for three target observables ( , , and ) in O+O at TeV and 200 GeV and in +Au at GeV. Most of the nonflow is removed, with residual fractions typically within 20%–30% when converted to the two-particle level, though the best estimator differs across the three targets. We identify a multiplicity-reweighting correction, previously overlooked in two-particle correlations, that explains the long-standing undersubtraction of the naive -scaling method; its impact grows as a power of the correlator order. The framework gives a systematic route to nonflow subtraction beyond two-particle correlations, broadening the class of multi-particle observables accessible to the small-system flow program.
tldr: The paper develops a general framework for subtracting nonflow contributions from multi-particle flow cumulants in small collision systems, using HIJING as a nonflow-only testbed.
motivation: Establishing collective flow in small systems is a prerequisite for determining minimal conditions for quark-gluon plasma formation, but multi-particle collectivity has been unverified at low multiplicity because residual nonflow in higher-order cumulants was never quantified.
method: The authors build a nonflow subtraction framework for n-particle cumulants based on approximate scaling of nonflow in the independent-source picture, using correlators containing k=2 as nonflow-dominated estimators and testing against three target observables in O+O and p+Au collisions with HIJING simulations.
result: Most nonflow is removed, with residual fractions typically 20%-30% at the two-particle level, and the best estimator varies across targets; a previously overlooked multiplicity-reweighting correction explains the long-standing undersubtraction of naive 1/N-scaling and grows with correlator order.
conclusion: The framework provides a systematic route to nonflow subtraction beyond two-particle correlations, broadening the class of multi-particle observables accessible to small-system flow studies.
